There are two routes to the potential of an extended distribution, and they are good for different things.

Route Use it when Section
\(V = k_e\displaystyle\int\frac{dq}{r}\) — sum contributions the geometry is simple and you have no field yet §24.6, below
\(\Delta V = -\displaystyle\int\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}\) — integrate a known field Gauss’s Law already gave you \(\vec{E}\) §24.6, “the other route”

The first builds \(V\) from charge. The second builds \(V\) from a field you already did the work to find. Recognising which one is cheaper is most of the skill.

Route 1 — Summing Contributions

Chop the distribution into elements \(dq\), each contributing \(k_e\,dq/r\), and add:

\[\boxed{\;V = k_e\int\frac{dq}{r}\;}\]

Compare this with the corresponding field integral, which needs components and unit vectors. Here there is one scalar integrand and no directions to track — often the difference between a problem you can do and one you cannot.

Uniformly Charged Ring

Ring of radius \(a\), total charge \(Q\), field point P on the axis at distance \(x\).

Every element is the same distance from P, \(r = \sqrt{a^2+x^2}\). That constant comes straight out of the integral:

\[V = k_e\int\frac{dq}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}} = \frac{k_e}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}\int dq\]

\[\boxed{\;V = \frac{k_e Q}{\sqrt{a^2+x^2}}\;}\]

There was no integral to do. The geometry did the work — which is the payoff of choosing a distribution whose every element sits at one distance.

Get the field by differentiating.

\[E_x = -\frac{dV}{dx} = -\frac{d}{dx}\left(k_eQ\left(a^2+x^2\right)^{-1/2}\right) = \frac{k_eQx}{\left(a^2+x^2\right)^{3/2}}\]

This is exactly the ring field from Chapter 23, which took a vector setup, a symmetry argument to kill the perpendicular component, and an integral. Here it is one derivative of a result that required no integration at all.

Check the limits as before: at \(x=0\) the numerator vanishes, so \(E = 0\) at the center — but note \(V = k_eQ/a\) there, its maximum. The potential is largest exactly where the field is zero, because zero field means zero slope, and a smooth function with zero slope is at a turning point. For \(x \gg a\), \(E \rightarrow k_eQ/x^2\) and \(V \rightarrow k_eQ/x\): a point charge, as it must be.

Uniformly Charged Disk

Radius \(R\), uniform surface density \(\sigma\), field point on the axis at \(x\). Build the disk out of rings — each of radius \(r\) and thickness \(dr\) carries \(dq = \sigma\left(2\pi r\,dr\right)\) and we already know a ring’s potential:

\[V = \int_0^R \frac{k_e\left(2\pi\sigma r\,dr\right)}{\sqrt{r^2+x^2}} = 2\pi k_e\sigma\int_0^R\frac{r\,dr}{\sqrt{r^2+x^2}}\]

\[\boxed{\;V = 2\pi k_e\sigma\left(\sqrt{R^2+x^2}-x\right) = \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(\sqrt{R^2+x^2}-x\right)\;}\]

Note the method: the ring was not an end in itself. It was built to be the element of the disk, exactly as the disk will be the element of other things. This is the same escalation you used in Chapter 23.

The infinite-sheet limit. Let \(R \gg x\) — stand very close to a very large disk. Then \(\sqrt{R^2+x^2}\rightarrow R\), and

\[V \rightarrow \frac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}\left(R - x\right)\]

so \(E_x = -dV/dx = \sigma/2\varepsilon_0\): constant, independent of distance, which is precisely the infinite-plane result from Gauss’s Law in §23.5. Two completely different routes — a flux argument and an axial integral — meeting at the same number is the strongest kind of check available.

Finite Line of Charge

A rod of length \(\ell\) carries \(Q\) uniformly, \(\lambda = Q/\ell\), lying along the \(x\)-axis from \(0\) to \(\ell\); P sits at height \(a\) above the near end.

\[V = k_e\lambda\int_0^\ell\frac{dx}{\sqrt{x^2+a^2}} = k_e\lambda\Big[\ln\left(x+\sqrt{x^2+a^2}\right)\Big]_0^\ell\]

\[\boxed{\;V = k_e\frac{Q}{\ell}\ln\left(\frac{\ell+\sqrt{\ell^2+a^2}}{a}\right)\;}\]

Far away, \(a \gg \ell\): expanding the logarithm gives \(V \approx k_eQ/a\) — a point charge again, as any bounded distribution must be from far enough off.

The logarithm is the signature of a line. You met it in Chapter 23 as the \(1/r\) field of a line charge; integrate \(1/r\) and you get \(\ln r\). Whenever a logarithm appears in an electrostatics answer, look for a one-dimensional source.

Route 2 — Integrating a Known Field

When Gauss’s Law has already handed you \(\vec{E}\), do not go back to the charge. Integrate the field you have:

\[V_B - V_A = -\int_A^B \vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s}\]

This is the same relation used in §24.3, but nothing now requires \(\vec{E}\) to be uniform. Whatever position-dependence the field carries goes straight into the integral.

Warm-Up: A Field That Grows With Distance

Before the radial cases, take the simplest non-uniform field there is. A region contains \(\vec{E} = Cx\,\hat{i}\) with \(C = 400\ \text{N}/(\text{C}\cdot\text{m})\). Find \(\Delta V\) between \(x_a = 0.500\ \text{m}\) and \(x_b = 1.50\ \text{m}\), moving along the \(x\)-axis.

Along the axis \(d\vec{s} = dx\,\hat{i}\), so \(\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s} = \left(Cx\right)dx\) and the integral is a polynomial:

\[\Delta V = -\int_{x_a}^{x_b} Cx\,dx = -C\left[\frac{x^2}{2}\right]_{x_a}^{x_b}\]

\[\boxed{\;\Delta V = -\frac{C}{2}\left(x_b^{2} - x_a^{2}\right) = -400\ \text{V}\;}\]

Two checks, both cheap. The displacement is along \(\vec{E}\), so \(V\) must fall — and it does. And because \(E\) is linear in \(x\), its average across the interval equals its value at the midpoint: \(E(1.00\ \text{m}) = 400\) N/C, and a uniform \(400\ \text{N/C}\) over \(\Delta x = 1.00\) m gives \(-400\) V, exactly the integral’s answer.

That shortcut is not general. It worked only because \(E\) is linear; for the \(1/r\) fields below, the midpoint value is not the average and the trick fails. Knowing when a shortcut is licensed is worth more than the shortcut.

Between Two Coaxial Conductors

An inner conductor of radius \(a\) and a concentric outer shell of radius \(b\), both of length \(\ell\), carry \(+Q\) and \(-Q\). Find the potential difference between them.

Step 1 — get the field from Gauss’s Law. A coaxial cylindrical surface of radius \(r\), with \(a<r<b\) and length \(\ell\), encloses \(Q\). By cylindrical symmetry \(\vec{E}\) is radial and constant on that surface, and the end caps carry no flux:

\[E\left(2\pi r\ell\right) = \frac{Q}{\varepsilon_0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E(r) = \frac{Q}{2\pi\varepsilon_0 \ell\, r} = \frac{2k_e\lambda}{r}\]

with \(\lambda = Q/\ell\). The field falls as \(1/r\) — the infinite-line result of §23.5, which is what a long coaxial cable looks like from inside the gap.

Step 2 — integrate it inward. Walk radially from \(b\) to \(a\), so \(d\vec{s} = dr\,\hat{r}\) and \(\vec{E}\cdot d\vec{s} = E\,dr\):

\[V_a - V_b = -\int_b^a \frac{2k_e\lambda}{r}\,dr = 2k_e\lambda\int_a^b\frac{dr}{r}\]

\[\boxed{\;\Delta V = V_a - V_b = 2k_e\lambda\ln\!\left(\frac{b}{a}\right)\;}\]

Where the logarithm came from, and why it had to. Nothing was integrated by brute force — \(\int dr/r = \ln r\), and that is the only place a logarithm can enter. Trace it back: the log is here because the field went as \(1/r\), and the field went as \(1/r\) because the source is effectively one-dimensional.

Contrast a spherical geometry, where \(E \sim 1/r^2\) integrates to \(1/a - 1/b\) — a difference of reciprocals, no logarithm anywhere. The functional form of a potential difference is a fingerprint of the source’s dimensionality, and you can predict which form you will get before doing the integral.

Sign check. \(b>a\) makes \(\ln(b/a)>0\), so \(V_a > V_b\): the inner conductor, carrying the positive charge, sits at the higher potential. Correct — and note the check cost nothing but reading the sign of a logarithm.

Limiting case. As \(b \rightarrow a\) the gap closes, \(\ln(b/a)\rightarrow 0\), and \(\Delta V \rightarrow 0\). Two conductors pressed together cannot hold a potential difference, which is what a short circuit is.

Why this one matters. \(\Delta V\) is proportional to \(Q\) — double the charge and you double the potential difference, because \(\lambda\) appears linearly and the geometry factor \(\ln(b/a)\) does not care about charge at all. That fixed ratio \(Q/\Delta V\) depends only on the geometry, and in Chapter 25 it is given a name: capacitance.
